Further, we compare our approach with two recent methods that address the oversmoothing problem. The approach in [ 8] directly addresses oversmoothing in GCNs by using partially absorbing random walks [28] to mitigate rapid mixing of node features in highly connected graph regions. The graph attention network (GAT) [10] indirectly addresses oversmoothing by training adaptive node-wise weighting of the smoothing operation via an attention mechanism. Furthermore, we also include two alternatives to GCN networks based on Chebyshev polynomial ﬁlters [20] and belief propagation of label information [29] computed via Gaussian random ﬁelds. Finally, we include two baseline approaches to verify the contribution of our hybrid approach compared to compared to the classiﬁer from [13] that is solely based on handcrafted graph-scattering features, and compared to SVM classiﬁer acting directly on node features without considering graph edges, which does not incorporate any geometric information. The methods from [4, 8, 10, 20, 29] were all executed using the original implementations accompa- nying their publications. These are tuned and evaluated using the standard splits provided for the benchmark datasets for fair comparison. We ensure that the reported classiﬁcation accuracies agree with previously published results when available. The tuning of our method (including hyperparame- ters and composition of GCN and scattering channels) on each dataset was done via grid search (over a ﬁxed set of choices for all datasets) using the same cross validation setup used to tune competing methods. For further details, we refer the reader to the supplement, which contains an ablation study evaluating the importance of each component in our proposed architecture. We discuss and consider richer notions of regularity on graphs to expand the GCN approach, which solely relies on enforcing smoothness over graph neighborhoods. This is achieved by incorporating multiple frequency bands of graph signals, which are typically not leveraged in traditional GCN models. Our construction is inspired by geometric scattering, which has mainly been used for whole-graph classiﬁcation so far. Our results demonstrate several beneﬁts of incorporating the elements presented here (i.e., scattering channels and residual convolutions) into GCN architectures. Furthermore, we expect the incorporation of these elements together in more intricate architectures to provide new capabilities of pattern recognition and local information extraction in graphs. For example, attention mechanisms could be used to adaptively tune scattering conﬁgurations at the resolution of each node, rather than the global graph level used here. C Further Discussion of Related Work As many applied ﬁelds such as Bioinformatics and Neuroscience heavily rely on the analysis of graph- structured data, the study of reliable classiﬁcation methods has received much attention lately. In this work, we focus on the particular class of semi-supervised classiﬁcation tasks, where GCN models [4, 8] recently proved to be effective. Their theoretical studies reveal however that graph convolutions can be interpreted as Laplacian smoothing operations, which poses fundamental limitations on the approach. Another branch of GNNs, manifested in [ 10], introduces self-attention mechanisms to determine adequate node-wise neighborhoods, which in turn alleviate the mentioned shortcomings of GCN approaches. Further, [9] developed a theoretical framework based on graph signal processing, relying on the relation between frequency and feature noise, to show that GNNs perform a low-pass ﬁltering on the feature vectors. In [31], multiple powers of the adjacency matrix were used to learn the higher-order neighborhood information, while [22] used Lanczos algorithm to construct a low-rank approximation of the graph Laplacian that efﬁciently gathers multiscale information, demonstrated on citation networks and the QM8 quantum chemistry dataset. Finally, [32] studied wavelets on graphs and collected higher-order neighborhood information based on wavelet transformation. Together with the study of learned networks, recent studies have also introduced the construction of geometric scattering transforms, relying on manually crafted families of graph wavelet transforms [11– 13]. Similar to the initial motivation of geometric deep learning to generalize convolutional neural networks, the geometric scattering framework generalizes the construction of Euclidean scattering from [14] to the graph setting. Theoretical studies [e.g., 11, 33, 25] established energy preservation properties and the stability of these generalized scattering transforms to perturbations and deforma- tions of graphs and signals on them. Moreover, the practical application of geometric scattering to whole-graph data analysis was studied in [ 12], achieving strong classiﬁcation results on social networks and biochemistry data, which established the effectiveness of this approach. As discussed in the main paper, this work aims to combine the complementary strengths of GCN models and geometric scattering and to provide a new avenue for incorporating richer notions of regularity in GNNs. Further, our construction integrates trained task-driven components in geometric scattering architectures. Finally, while most previous work on geometric scattering focused on whole-graph settings, we consider node-level processing, which requires new considerations about the construction. D Technical Details Similar to other neural networks, the presented Scattering GCN poses several architecture choices and hyperparameters that can be tuned and affect its performance. For simplicity, we set the last layer before the output classiﬁcation to be the residual convolution layer and only consider one or two 15hybrid layers before it, each consisting of three GCN channels and two scattering channels. We note that this restricted setup simpliﬁes the network tuning process and was sufﬁcient in our experiments to obtain promising results (outperforming other methods, as shown in the main paper), but can naturally be generalized further to deeper or wider architectures in practice. Furthermore, based on preliminary results, Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed were set to use only one hybrid layer as the addition of a second one was not cost-effective (considering the added complexity of a grid search for tuning hyperparameters based on validation results). For DBLP, two layers were used due to a signiﬁcant increase in performance. We note that even with a single hybrid layer our model achieves 73.1% test accuracy (compared to the reported 81.5% for two layers) and still signiﬁcantly outperforms GAT (66.1%) and the other methods (below 60%). Validation & testing procedure: All tests were done using train-validation-test splits of the datasets, where validation accuracy is used for tuning hyperparameters and test accuracy is re- ported in the comparison table. The same splits were used for all methods for a fair comparison. To ensure our evaluation is comparable with previous work, for Citeseer, Cora and Pubmed we used the same settings as in [4], following the standard practice used in other work reporting results on these datasets. For DBLP, as far as we know, no common standard is established in the literature. Here, we used a ratio of 5 : 1 : 1between train, validation, and test. The grid covered the tuning of the residual convolution viaα, the nonlinarity exponent q (inspired by scattering moments), the scattering channel conﬁguration (i.e., scales used in these two channels), and the widths of channels in the network. E Ablation Study The two main components of our Scattering GCN architecture contribute together to achieve signiﬁ- cant improvements over pure GCN models. Namely, these are the additional scattering channels (i.e., UJ1 and UJ2 ) and the residual convolution (controlled by the hyperparemeter α). To further explore their contribution and the hyperparameter space for their tuning, Tab. 3-7 show classiﬁcation results over the Cora dataset for α = 0.01,0.1,0.35,0.5,1.0 (controlling the residual convolution layer) over multiple scattering channel conﬁgurations. For presentation brevity and simplicity, we focus our 16presented ablation benchmark on this dataset here, but note that similar results are also observed on the other datasets. The rows and columns in each table denote the two scattering channels used in the Scattering GCN, together with the three GCN channels (i.e., for Ak, k= 1,2,3). First, we consider the importance of the residual graph convolution layer. We note that setting α= 0 effectively ignores this layer (i.e., by setting its operation to be the identity), while increasing α makes the ﬁltering provided by it to be more dominant until α = 1, where it essentially becomes a random walk-based low-pass ﬁlter. Therefore, to evaluate the importance of this component of our architecture, it is sufﬁcient to evaluate the impact of αon the classiﬁcation accuracy. Indeed, our results (see Tab. 3-7) indicate that increasing α to non-negligible nonzero values improves classiﬁcation performance, which we interpret to be due to the removal of high-frequency noise. However, when αfurther increases (in particular when α= 1in this case) the smoothing provided by this layer degrades the performance to a level close to the traditional GCN [4]. Therefore, these results suggest that when well tuned (e.g., as done via grid search in this work), the graph residual convolution plays a critical role in improving results, which can also be seen by the results of the hyperparameter tuning shown in the previous section. Next, we consider the scales used in the two scattering channels of our hybrid architecture, which correspond to the rows and columns of Tab. 3-7 here. While our results show that the network is relatively robust to this choice, we can observe that generally utilizing purely second-order coefﬁcients gives slightly worse results than either ﬁrst-order ones or a mix of ﬁrst- and second-order coefﬁcients. Nevertheless, most conﬁgurations of scattering scales (with appropriate choice of α) give better results than pure GCN, thus indicating that added information is extracted by scattering channels. We note that for α = 0.35 (Tab. 5), all scale conﬁgurations outperform GAT (83%) and all other reported methods in Tab. 2 (of the main paper). As a result, even the average accuracy over all scale conﬁgurations (83.5%) in this case shows an improvement over these other methods, thus further establishing the advantage of our approach. It is important to mention that while this improvement is affected by the tuning of the residual convolution, it also relies on the addition of scattering channels. Indeed, by itself, the residual convolution layer only applies a low-pass (smoothing) ﬁlter and therefore, without scattering channels, would essentially be equivalent to a conventional GCN. Finally, to further validate the importance of band-pass information added by the presented architec- ture here, we provide an ablation study of the impact each channel has on classiﬁcation performance. We focus here on α= 0.35 with the best conﬁguration on Cora (i.e., achieving 84.2% accuracy when all channels are used). Then, we remove each of the band-pass or low-pass channels individually from the network, and reevaluate network performance with the remaining four channels. Our results, presented in Tab. 8, indicate that while information captured byA,A2 and A3 is important for the classiﬁcation task, which is to be expected given the prevalence of such ﬁlters in GCNs, the band-pass information extracted by the scattering channels (with Ψ2 and Ψ1 in this case) plays a crucial role in achieving the performance of our method. In particular, we note that Ψ1 in this case has a major impact on the accuracy, driving the difference between underperforming and outperforming GAT, thus strengthening the claim that important information in graph features is contained in higher frequencies extracted by band-pass ﬁltering, which is not recovered by smoothing operations. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: This paper proposes Scattering GCN, a novel approach to overcome the oversmoothing problem in Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) for semi-supervised node classification tasks. The core contribution is augmenting conventional GCNs with geometric scattering transforms, which enable band-pass filtering of graph signals, and graph residual convolutions to clear high-frequency noise. The work establishes theoretical advantages by demonstrating how scattering and GCN features complement each other and shows superior experimental results against leading graph neural networks, particularly on datasets with higher connectivity where oversmoothing is more pronounced.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The methodology combines low-pass operations from GCNs with band-pass operations from geometric scattering networks. GCN operations are defined as Hℓ = σ(A^k Hℓ-1 Θℓ + Bℓ) using different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix A. Geometric scattering on graphs is adapted to the node level, using wavelet matrices (Ψk) and pointwise absolute value nonlinearities to create scattering transforms (Up), with a propagation rule Hℓ = σ(Up Hℓ-1 Θℓ + Bℓ). A hybrid network architecture concatenates these GCN and scattering channels. A 'graph residual convolution' layer (Ares(α) = 1/(α+1) (In + αWD^-1)) is introduced after the hybrid layer to reduce high-frequency noise, acting as a tunable low-pass filter via hyperparameter α. The nonlinearity σ(.) := |.|q is used, applied at the node-level.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The Scattered GCN was evaluated on semi-supervised node classification tasks using four benchmark graph datasets: Citeseer, Cora, Pubmed, and DBLP, which vary in size, connectivity, and feature informativeness. Performance was compared against GCN, Graph Attention Networks (GAT), Partially Absorbing Random Walks, Chebyshev polynomial filters, Label Propagation, a pure graph scattering baseline, and a non-geometric linear SVM baseline using only node features. All comparison methods used their original implementations and standard data splits. Hyperparameter tuning (including α, nonlinearity exponent q, scattering channel configurations, and channel widths) was performed via grid search using cross-validation, guided by validation accuracy. The experiments were conducted on an HPC cluster with an Intel i7-6850K CPU and NVIDIA TITAN X Pascal GPU, with Scattering GCN implemented in PyTorch.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The architecture used in the experiments was limited to one or two hybrid layers (each with three GCN and two scattering channels) to simplify tuning, implying that deeper or wider architectures might offer further improvements. The hyperparameter tuning for the DBLP dataset was less exhaustive compared to others, potentially yielding a lower bound on its performance. The theoretical studies of geometric information encoding in graph wavelets were not extensive and are left for future work. The model, while robust, requires careful tuning of hyperparameters like α for the residual convolution and the scales of scattering channels for optimal performance.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future research could involve incorporating more intricate architectures, such as attention mechanisms, to adaptively tune scattering configurations at the resolution of each node, rather than globally. Further theoretical studies are needed to understand the geometric information encoding properties of graph wavelets. A more intensive and exhaustive study of specific datasets like DBLP, with potentially more comprehensive architectural and hyperparameter optimization, is also suggested.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Most anti-oversmoothing techniques either (i) apply a *global* remedy (normalization layers, residual shortcuts, edge dropping) or (ii) pre/post-process features with a *fixed* node–specific depth that is **not learned end-to-end** (e.g. NDLS).  As a result:  1) the same propagation depth is still used for all nodes during training, ignoring that the optimal depth changes *dynamically* with the node state and with model parameters; 2) pre-/post-processing solutions break privacy guarantees and prevent joint optimisation of depth and weights; 3) existing metrics (row-diff, GIns/RGroup) are used only for diagnosis, not as training signals.  The key open problem is therefore:  “How can we design a *fully differentiable, node-adaptive and privacy-preserving* mechanism that **learns during training when each node should stop aggregating messages**, thereby maximising the useful denoising effect while preventing class-mixing?”
Methods: We propose Dynamic Halting Graph Neural Network (DH-GNN).  Core ideas:  1. Layer-wise Halting Controller  –  Each node i keeps a scalar  h_i^ℓ∈(0,1)  that is the probability of *halting* message passing after layer ℓ.  A tiny MLP that takes the current hidden state H_i^ℓ, its initial feature X_i and a 2-hop degree sketch outputs h_i^ℓ using a Gumbel-Sigmoid, enabling re-parameterised gradients.  2. Adaptive Aggregation  –  At layer ℓ each node combines standard message passing M_i^ℓ  (GCN, GAT, etc.) and its own frozen representation R_i = H_i^{τ(i)} where τ(i) is the first layer in which it decided to halt.  Concretely  H_i^{ℓ+1} = (1−z_i^ℓ)·M_i^ℓ + z_i^ℓ·R_i   with  z_i^ℓ∼Bernoulli(h_i^ℓ).  3. Oversmoothing-aware Regulariser  –  We add a loss term  L_mix = Σ_i max(0, MDR_i −γ) where MDR_i is the *local mixing–denoising ratio* computed from neighbours’ embeddings (uses means & variances but is differentiable via stop-gradient on variance). γ is a target threshold.  This pushes the controller to halt when class mixing starts to dominate.  4. Budget Penalty  –  Σ_i τ(i) is softly penalised to avoid every node propagating to the maximum depth.  5. Privacy Safety  –  Because depth decisions and representations never leave the network, no smoothed features are exposed.  6. Plug-and-Play  –  The controller is architecture agnostic and introduces <2% extra parameters; it can wrap any message-passing backbone (GCN, GAT, GCNII, SAGE).  Differences to prior work: (a) unlike NDLS the depth is *learned jointly* with weights; (b) unlike DGN/PairNorm it changes *how far* messages travel rather than how they are normalised; (c) no external graph rewiring or feature release, so no leakage.
Experimental Setup: Datasets  –  Homophilous: Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, ogbn-arxiv.  Heterophilous: Chameleon, Squirrel, Actor.  Large-scale: ogbn-papers100M (10% sample).  Missing-feature variant: randomly mask 50% of test node features.  Baselines  –  4-layer and 32-layer versions of GCN, GAT, GCNII; GCN+PairNorm, GCN+DGN, GCN+DropEdge; NDLS (with MLP); PSNR; and a fixed-depth *oracle* that scans depths on validation.  Metrics  –  (i) Node classification accuracy; (ii) Group Distance Ratio & Instance Information Gain; (iii) row-diff & col-diff; (iv) proposed Local Mixing-Denoising Ratio (MDR); (v) average effective depth ⟨τ⟩ and inference FLOPs.  Ablations  –  Remove halting regulariser, remove budget term, replace Gumbel-Sigmoid with deterministic threshold.  Robustness  –  (1) feature-masking; (2) edge perturbation (10% random deletions); (3) transfer the learned controller to unseen graphs with similar statistics.  Implementation  –  PyTorch Geometric; training with Adam, 1000 epochs, 10 runs per setting, early stopping on validation accuracy.
Result: We expect DH-GNN to  • achieve +1.5 – 4.0% accuracy over the best non-adaptive deep baselines on homophilous data at ≥16 layers, and similar gains (≥2%) on heterophilous graphs where over-smoothing starts earlier;  • keep ⟨τ⟩ between 4 and 10 regardless of maximum layer count 64, cutting inference cost by ~40%;  • lower median MDR below γ across all nodes, while baselines exceed it after 8 layers;  • surpass NDLS under missing-feature and edge-perturbation tests because decisions are data-driven, not graph-dependent hyper-parameters;  • ablation shows ∼60% of the gain comes from the halting controller, 25% from L_mix, remainder from budget regulariser.
Conclusion: DH-GNN offers the first *fully differentiable, node-adaptive halting* mechanism for message passing, unifying depth selection with weight learning.  It mitigates oversmoothing without sacrificing denoising, reduces computation, and preserves privacy by avoiding external feature release.  Beyond node classification, the idea of learnable halting can be extended to link prediction, graph-level tasks and continual learning on streaming graphs.  Future work may integrate uncertainty-aware controllers, explore co-training with spectral pruning for over-squashing, and investigate theoretical bounds on depth distributions learned by DH-GNN.
